@@70645558 <h> Alarming trends continue in latest UN climate report <p> Ocean temperatures reached a record high last year , extreme weather events are exacerbating world hunger , and the world is not on track to meet emissions reduction targets , a new report says . <p> Photo : AFP <p> The latest state of the climate report by the World Meteorological Organisation said the effects of climate change were accelerating to dangerous levels , and were being felt in the Pacific . <p> The report , with contributions from dozens of scientists , UN agencies and national weather authorities including Fiji , Australia and New Zealand , also said greenhouse gas emissions had risen to unprecedented levels . <p> It showed sea levels were on the rise , and the water was warmer and increasingly acidic , which threatened to destabilise whole ecosystems . <p> And there were no signs the warming trend , which began at the start of this century , will ease . <p> The UN body 's report comes ahead of a summit in September that 's been billed as a last-chance opportunity for leaders to tackle climate change . 
@@70645716 <h> Book reviews : Fragment and Rage Becomes Her <h> Fragment by Craig Russell ( Thistledown Press , $22 ) <p> Climate change and its likely impact is the key focus of our age . US President Donald Trump 's ostrich-like denial only serves to increase the attention . So , it was only predictable that the subject would enter the domain of fiction . <p> Canadian author Craig Russell has a fertile imagination . His take on our changing world features a gigantic slab of ice that breaks off the Antarctic sheet . It is so enormous that it is unstoppable , crushing everything it encounters , even establishing its own micro-climate . So far , so plausible . We have even seen stray icebergs float past the South Island . <p> Russell 's eco-thriller , however , is not big on plausibility . Aimed at a late teenage market , it is alarmist in its tone and sensationalist in its narrative . First published in Canada in 2016 , it has just been released here , presumably because one of its many protagonists is a " Maori scientist " , although you would never guess that . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ cast of thousands to track the progress of this giant ice cube . These characters range from glaciologists , scientists , submarine crew , TV reporters , marketing executives , carpet salesmen , admirals , bomber pilots , boat charterers , Pentagon officials and so on . Even the President gets a scene , in which he reveals he is possibly ( but only possibly ) more ignorant and bigoted than the present incumbent . <p> In a cataclysmic rush , the ice fragment charges up the South Atlantic , heading past the tropics and into the Gulf of Mexico , where it wreaks immense damage . Russell 's prose is breathless , as he records people shot out of a submarine 's tubes in the Antarctic Ocean , surfacing right next to a yacht which has just patched a hole in a sinking cruiseliner . Credibility and plausibility are junked early on in a mad scramble for the lifeboats ! It is as if Titanic has met Independence Day in a competition for the end of the world . The whole book ends in a riot of uncontrolled imagination @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Kiwi scientist who helps save the day . And it is all because he has learnt how to speak Whale ! Yes , our non-te reo speaker has decoded cetacean-speak and communicates with one handily surfing before the ice-cube . Neat , eh ! <p> Russell 's own focus is extremely diffuse . He darts from one situation to the next , often devoting just a page to each . Likewise , characterisation is also sketchy , at best . <p> In a competitive market for young adult fiction , it is a real pity that teenagers are not fed more substantial material . It does them no service to load them with saccharine cliches from sub-Hollywood plot lines . The final insult is to end with a sermon , in case they missed the point behind this torrent of tosh . -- Steve Walker <p> Fifty-six per cent of men , according to a 2016 American study , believe sexism has been eradicated from daily life . Read that again . More than a quarterof the population genuinely believes sexism is a thing of the past . <p> Does @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ would you feel comfortable standing up and saying , loud and clear , that it makes you angry ? <p> Probably not , says Soraya Chemaly . In Rage Becomes Her , the activist and writer sets out to prove that sexism is very real and that we have every reason to be enraged by it . She demonstrates how women 's anger is systematically silenced as a way to maintain the status quo . And she encourages us to reclaim our anger and use it as an instrument for change . <p> The statistic I led with is one of hundreds that Chemaly cites , relating to all aspects of modern life . ( Most of the studies are American ; depressingly , we can assume attitudes are more or less the same throughout the Western world . ) Parents pay boys 13 per cent more pocket money than girls . Men hold over 70 per cent of the roles in top US films . More than half of Americans think women should be legally required to take their husbands ' last names . Men 's emergency room wait @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ women 's . Male Supreme Court justices interrupt their female colleagues three times as often as they do each other . <p> Just one of those figures should be enough to make your blood boil ; reading them all , page after page , is maddening in the extreme . But , as Chemaly says , we 've been conditioned to suppress this feeling , causing severe harm to ourselves in the process : " The unfairnesses that we intuit and experience but can not ' prove ' , as we are asked to do so often , are more likely to become internalised anger rather than externalised action . " <p> Indeed . Being asked to repeatedly prove that your daily reality is , well , real is one of the most exhausting , disheartening parts of being a woman . So Chemaly does the job for us -- first of providing evidence , such as the stats above , and then of showing us how we can take action effectively , fuelled and informed by our anger . There 's even a 10-point plan for harnessing anger productively @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ text , not a self-help book designed to be easily digested and then promptly forgotten . Chemaly does occasionally slip into bad academic-writing habits , resulting in clunky sentences like this : " This socialisation makes the internalisation of objectification second nature in processes known as self-objectification and self-surveillance . " <p> Most of the time , though , Rage Becomes Her is an absorbing read and one that will stay with you . You 'll think of it every time you describe yourself as frustrated , stressed or disappointed instead of angry ; every time you hear a high-profile woman being described as crazy , bitchy or unlikeable for behaviour that would be praised in a man ; and every time you cry when you really want to yell. -- India Lopez

@@70646011 <h> Scientists consider earthquake warning system to help Kiwis prepare for tremor <p> Wellington 's central library closed on Tuesday night following advice received from engineers that the building may not be safe in the event of an earthquake . <p> Would New Zealanders benefit from a early warning system for earthquakes ? <p> Researchers from around the country are conducting a survey to identify whether a warning system should be implemented in New Zealand . <p> The Earthquake Early Warning Survey ( EEW ) , funded by the Earthquake Commission , is asking Kiwis what they would do if were warned about a strong earthquake approaching , and what type of early warning system would work best . <p> " The survey is being carried out to understand how New Zealanders would respond to an early warning without incoming earthquake shaking , " said lead researcher , Dr Julia Becker , from Massey University in Wellington . <p> Earthquake scientists , engineers and various social scientists from Massey University , GNS Science , and the University of Auckland are working to understand what Kiwis expect from such system . <p> " We also want to find out how @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ what is the minimum strength of shaking would they want to be warned about and how would they like to receive the warning , " Becker said . <p> The detection system works off the two waves sent by the earthquake -- P-waves and S-waves -- before a tremor is felt . Becker likens these waves to how we usually see lightning before we hear thunder . <p> " With an earthquake , the P-waves travel very fast and are picked up by sensors first , automatically sending an alert to locations further away warning them to expect strong earthquake shaking , " Becker said . <p> " The S-waves that cause the shaking and damage travel more slowly , so unless you 're at the centre of the earthquake , you can get a warning of what is coming . " <p> GEONET <p> On Sunday evening , the Wellington region was hit with a magnitude 3.6 earthquake . <p> Currently , Japan , Mexico and Taiwan all have early detection systems in place , with some sending out warnings from mere seconds up to two minutes before shaking @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ hospitals , rail and road transport , and education , researchers are trying to see how various sectors would benefit from a warning system . <p> " We know for instance in Japan that train drivers slow down and surgeons make patients safe during an operation once they receive a warning , " Becker said . <p> This particular type of system presents a number of benefits for the community , but researchers will need to conduct " other studies on the economic and engineering aspects " before seriously considering implementing it in New Zealand . <p> The survey is considered an appropriate first step to gauge how the public would react to this particular warning system . <p> EQC 's Director of Resilience Research , Dr Hugh Cowan , supports the need for a public survey .
